text: Every matrix you've multiplied so far has rotated, stretched, or sheared vectors into new directions. This lesson introduces the special vectors a matrix does not turn — it only stretches or shrinks them — and that idea turns out to be the mathematical backbone of what a quantum measurement actually is.

For almost any vector, multiplying by a matrix points it in a different direction. An eigenvector is the exception: a nonzero vector v such that A v equals lambda v for some scalar lambda, called the eigenvalue. The output is the same vector, just scaled — same direction, or exactly reversed if lambda is negative, with no rotation at all. Lambda can be real, complex, negative, or zero.

Take A equals 3,1,0,2. Multiply it by 1,0 and you get 3,0 — exactly 3 times the original vector, so 1,0 is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. Now multiply A by 1,1 and you get 4,2. Is that some single number times 1,1? Four over one is four, but two over one is two — two different ratios, so there's no single lambda that works. 1,1 is not an eigenvector; it got rotated into a genuinely different direction, not just scaled.

A matrix has only a handful of these special directions, and along them, its complicated action collapses down to multiplying by a single number — the eigenvalue, a property of the matrix itself. In quantum computing, the operators representing measurable physical quantities have their own set of these directions, and their eigenvalues are literally the only numbers a measurement can ever return. There's no quantum magic in that — it's this same linear-algebra idea, applied to the matrices quantum mechanics happens to use.
Next lesson shows you how to find these eigenvalues and eigenvectors from scratch, rather than just checking a candidate — using the single most important gate matrix in quantum computing, Pauli-Z.
